events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Noah proposes Noah, Lucia. I’ll join Lucia for the first mission; with no prior results, this is an initial team to test.

I have reservations about this team. Noah has put himself and Lucia forward with no prior results, and that gives us little reason to trust the choice. Since this is our first mission, I'd like to see a team that gives the table more balance and a clearer rationale than a leader selecting himself. I'm inclined to reject this proposal unless someone can explain why this pairing is the best option.

I'm going to vote against this team. Noah has put himself on it, and Lucia is the only other name, with no results to justify either of them. A first mission is when the table most needs a team built on reasons, not self-selection. Noah, if you revise, I'd like you to explain why you chose Lucia over the other three players, and to include someone who isn't defending their own place. I'd also welcome Omar or Arjun offering a rationale for a different pairing before we vote.

Theo, I chose Lucia without any prior evidence; the pairing is a starting point, not a claim of proven trust. Including myself gives me one place I can personally account for, and any first team necessarily involves an untested choice. I’m inclined to keep it and let the result and votes give us information.

I will be voting against this team. Noah and Lucia together form a pairing with no mission results behind it, and I am not willing to send both into a first mission on that basis. Noah, your answer that the pairing is only a starting point does not explain why the table should accept a team that leaves out Omar, Arjun, and me. Arjun, what pairing would you propose instead, and why would it serve the mission better than this one?

Thank you, Theo, for the question. I'll answer it directly. I don't find the self-selection objection as damaging as you do. On a first mission with zero results, every possible pairing is untested, and the leader has to choose someone; a leader including themselves is conventional and gives them personal accountability for the outcome. Rejecting a team simply because it is untested would reject every possible first team, including any alternative I named. So I don't currently see a pairing I could propose that would be more likely to succeed than this one — any two names from this table carry identical evidence right now. That said, I do share one smaller concern: as proposed, this team builds information about only two players, and the other three of us learn nothing about ourselves this round regardless of the outcome. If the leader is open to it, swapping one member — for example, bringing in Omar instead of Lucia — would not make the mission more likely to succeed, but it would spread the trust-building across more of the table and give us slightly more signal going into mission two. That is a marginal improvement, not a reason to force a rejection. Noah, would you be willing to revise the team to include Omar in place of Lucia, or do you have a specific reason for choosing Lucia in particular that you haven't shared with the table yet? If the answer is simply that the pairing was arbitrary, I'd rather we accept the team and let the result speak than burn proposals on a first mission where all options are equally unproven.

Arjun, the choice of Lucia was arbitrary, as I said; I have no specific reason to prefer her over Omar. Swapping one untested player for another doesn't give us more information on this mission, so I'm inclined to keep the team and let the result and votes inform us.

Theo, I want to push back on the framing of your objection, because I think it's being applied asymmetrically. You say a first mission should not be built on self-selection, but your alternative is that the leader must justify each name — and then Arjun and I are both told that no pairing could be better, since every option carries identical evidence. That is an argument that any team is as good as any other, and if any team is as good as any other, then rejecting this one does nothing but spend a proposal and a round of trust on a distinction the table has agreed doesn't exist.

Arjun's point about spreading information is well taken but it cuts the other way. Swapping Lucia for Omar would not create more signal from this mission; it would only change which single untested name is exposed to the result, and the table would still learn nothing about anyone else. The cost of the swap is a revision, a public fight, and the possibility that the leader's revision fails and the table burns another proposal on mission one with no results at all. The cost of accepting is zero — we find out about two players instead of one. If we want broad information, the natural place to get it is mission two, where the size grows and we can deliberately rotate.

Noah also answered your question directly and honestly: the pairing was arbitrary. That is the correct answer for a zero-information round, and I would rather have a leader who says plainly that a choice was arbitrary than one who manufactures a rationale after being challenged. Theo, you have every right to vote your conscience; I've only asked that you consider whether your objection is about this team specifically or about the fact that it is the first team. I don't think it can be about the first team, because you'd reject every proposal that followed.

My vote is to keep Noah and Lucia and to let the result speak. And if we accept that principle, I'd like us to agree on a second one: after this mission, we judge people on what the table has actually seen, not on who was persuasive in the discussion.

Theo, I want to be direct with you rather than diplomatic. Your objection is not about this team; it is about the fact that this is the first team, and I think you know that, because when Arjun laid out the logic clearly — every pairing is equally untested, and a leader including themselves is conventional and gives them personal accountability — you did not offer a single name you could argue is better. You have argued for a process, not for an alternative team, and that is precisely the process that lets any leader pick any two names and win approval. If we reject here over a distinction the table has already conceded does not exist, we teach the table that good-faith reasoning is punished and every future proposal gets the same treatment.

Let me also address what I believe is the actual substance underneath your position. You asked Noah to include "someone who isn't defending their own place." But Noah is on this team, and so am I, and we are two of the five people at this table with the least claim to untested positions — the first mission is exactly where an untested pair should be found out, not where we should pretend we have signal we do not have. Sending two people whose behavior we can actually observe is more informative than any reasoning about who "deserves" a seat before we have seen anyone act.

On the swap: Arjun suggested bringing in Omar for me, and I want to be plain that the information argument does not support it. A two-person mission reveals exactly two names. Swapping changes which name, not how many. The cost is a revision, a public fight, and real risk of a second proposal being burned on mission one with no result to inform it — the same outcome Theo is complaining about, arrived at by the route he recommends.

Noah, since you are the one who must decide whether to revise: are you planning to hold Noah and Lucia, or are you genuinely considering the swap to Omar? If you are considering it, I would like to hear you say what evidence would make the swap better than the team as it stands, because I do not believe any exists right now.

My vote is for Noah and Lucia, and I will not be moved by an objection that applies equally to every possible team and would therefore reject every possible team.

Lucia, I’m holding the team as proposed. My choice was arbitrary, and I don’t see a reason to swap one untested player for another. I’d rather let the vote and mission give us something concrete to work with.

Theo, I want to answer your objection one last time, and I want to do it without any diplomacy, because I think the table is about to make a decision based on a distinction that does not exist.

You have never named a single player you would put on this mission instead. Not one. When Arjun laid out the logic — that with zero results every pairing is equally untested, that a leader including himself is conventional and gives him personal accountability, and that rejecting an untested team rejects every possible first team — you did not offer an alternative. You have argued for a process, not for a team. And a process objection that applies to every possible proposal is not a safeguard; it is a veto. It means no team can ever be approved on mission one, whatever it contains. That is not careful deliberation, that is a refusal to decide.

I also want to be honest about what you asked Noah for. You asked him to include "someone who isn't defending their own place." But on a first mission, nobody has a place to defend. We have no results, no track record, nothing. The only thing a first team can do is put two observable people in a room and see what happens. Reasoning about who "deserves" a seat before any of us has done anything is not a higher standard, it is a fictional one.

On Arjun's swap suggestion: he was clear that it would not make the mission more likely to succeed, only marginally spread trust-building. Arjun, I agree with your framing that if the pairing was arbitrary, the right move is to accept it and let the result speak rather than burn proposals on a zero-information round. Swapping changes which single name is exposed, not how many, and it costs us a revision and the risk of another wasted proposal. Noah has answered you plainly — the choice was arbitrary, and no specific reason exists. I would rather have a leader who says that honestly than one who invents a rationale under pressure.

My vote is to keep Noah and Lucia. And I would ask the table to agree on the principle Lucia stated earlier: from mission two onward, we judge people on what we have actually seen, not on who was persuasive in the discussion. Right now we have seen nothing, and the only thing rejection buys us is a delay.

I’m not on this team, so I have no private reason to defend or reject it. On a first mission every pairing is untested; Noah has stated the choice was arbitrary, and I prefer that to an invented justification. Theo’s objection has not produced a concrete better pairing. Arjun’s suggested swap to me would change which untested name is exposed, not create more signal, and Noah has now clearly declined to revise. At this point the cost of rejecting is another proposal and delay with no new evidence. I intend to vote to approve Noah and Lucia so we get actual mission data. If it fails, the result itself will be the reason to scrutinize both team members next discussion; if it succeeds, that is useful but not proof. Arjun, since you raised the swap to me, do you now support holding Noah and Lucia and voting approve, or do you still think the swap is worth pursuing after Noah’s refusal?

Omar, you asked whether I support holding Noah and Lucia after Noah declined the swap, and my answer is yes. I raised the swap as a marginal improvement, not a condition of approval, and Noah has now answered plainly that his choice of Lucia was arbitrary and that he sees no reason to exchange one untested player for another. That is an honest answer, and I accept it. The swap would have changed which single name is exposed to this mission's result, not how many names we learn about, so its information value was always small. What matters more now is not spending proposals on a distinction nobody at this table has been able to turn into a concrete alternative. Theo has had multiple turns to name a better pairing and has not done so; his objection applies equally to every possible first team, which means accepting it would reject every possible first team. I will vote to approve Noah and Lucia. If the mission fails, the result itself becomes the reason to scrutinize both of them next round, and I will do exactly that — from mission two onward, I want us judging players on what we have actually observed rather than on who argued most persuasively. If it succeeds, that is useful signal but not proof, and I will hold the same standard for everyone. For now, approving is the fastest path to real data, and real data is what this table needs.
Noah confirms Noah, Lucia. I’m keeping Noah and Lucia as proposed; the choice was arbitrary, and the mission will provide our first result.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (2 fail cards).

Theo proposes Omar, Arjun, Theo. Mission 1 failed with Noah and Lucia on it, so I'm leaving both off and proposing Omar, Arjun, and myself. Omar and Arjun have each argued for accountability on the table, and I'm willing to share the risk of this mission.

Mission 1 gave us two fail cards from a two-person team, Noah and Lucia. That means both Noah and Lucia must be Evil. Theo's proposed team is Omar, Arjun, and Theo — exactly the three players who were not on that failed team. From my perspective, this is the cleanest available team, and I support approving it. I will vote approve.

The two fail cards establish that Lucia and I are Evil, so the proposed team is the only all-Good team available. I expect it to be approved. Theo, what specifically made you oppose the first team so strongly before its result?

Noah, you asked what made me oppose the first team so strongly. It was the reasoning, not the names. You chose yourself and Lucia and gave no rationale beyond calling the choice arbitrary. When I asked for a better explanation, the answer was that every pairing is equally untested, and Lucia pressed hard to keep the team and to frame my objection as a veto on every first team. A leader who calls his pick arbitrary and then defends it that forcefully should expect the table to want more than that. I had no proof on the first team. I did have a concern about a self-selected pair, and the failed mission has now put that concern on the record with both of them on it.

On this proposal: Omar, Arjun, and I are the three players who were not on the failed mission. Omar has argued for accountability, and Arjun has pushed for spreading trust-building across the table. I am willing to share the risk of this mission with them. The only two names attached to a fail card so far are Noah and Lucia, and they should stay off this mission while we gather more information.

Arjun, you said that if the mission failed, the result would be the reason to scrutinize the players on it, and that you would hold the same standard for everyone. Do you still hold that standard for this team, which has no results yet, and what would you need to see from the three of us before you would vote to approve it?

Theo, you asked whether I still hold the standard I set last round — that if Mission 1 failed, the result itself would be the reason to scrutinize the players on it. Yes, I do, and I will apply it right now. Mission 1 was a two-person team, Noah and Lucia, and it produced two fail cards. Two fail cards from a two-person team means both of them submitted fail. That is not suspicion or inference from rhetoric; it is arithmetic. Noah and Lucia are both Evil, and they should not go near a mission team again.

I want to be honest about my own record here. Last round I argued that any first pairing was equally untested and that approving was the fastest path to real data. That argument was wrong in one respect — I claimed every pairing carried identical evidence, and the fail count now tells us it did not — but the core recommendation was right: approving gave us the data, and the data is decisive. The exact outcome I committed to has happened. I said that if the mission failed I would scrutinize both team members next round, and I am doing exactly that. Both of them are off the table for this mission and for any future one unless something extraordinary surfaces.

This also reframes the vote record. Theo was the only player who voted against Noah and Lucia, and whatever his stated reasoning was at the time, his instinct was correct. Omar, Lucia, Noah, and I all approved a team containing two Evil players. I approved it on the reasoning that all pairings were equally unproven. That was a reasonable zero-information position, and I do not think anyone should be condemned for it — but it does mean the only current evidence distinguishing players is the mission result and the vote history, and both point the same way: Theo off the failed team, and Noah and Lucia on it with two fails.

Given that, the proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Theo is the only team consistent with everything we have observed: the three players not attached to fail cards. I am on it, I know I am Good, and I will play Success. I have no evidence against Omar or Theo — Omar argued for accountability and voted approve last round like I did, which we now know was a Good player's honest mistake, and Theo correctly opposed the Evil pair from the start.

Theo, one direct question before we finalize: as leader you have one revision available, and I want to confirm you are holding Omar, Arjun, and Theo exactly as proposed rather than considering any swap. If you are holding, I will vote approve, and I'd encourage everyone else to do the same so we bank a mission win while Noah and Lucia are fully exposed. If the mission somehow fails from here, my standard applies to me too — scrutinize me alongside Omar and Theo.

Arjun, yes, I am holding Omar, Arjun, and Theo exactly as proposed, and I will not swap anyone. The two fail cards on Noah and Lucia's mission are the clearest evidence we have. My objection to that pair was about the reasoning behind it. I asked Noah for a rationale, he answered that the choice was arbitrary, and the discussion then framed my concern as a veto on every first team. Noah and Lucia should stay off this mission. Omar, Arjun, and I were not on the failed team, so this is the proposal most consistent with what the table has observed. I ask everyone to approve it so we get a result while those two are kept off. If this mission fails, the same scrutiny should apply to all three of us, and the card count will show what happened.

I'll keep this short, because there is very little left to argue about and I don't want to spend proposals on a round where the arithmetic is already settled.

Mission 1 was a two-person team that failed with two Fail cards. Two Fail cards on a two-person team means both members submitted Fail. That is not a reading of rhetoric, it is a count. Noah and Lucia are therefore confirmed Evil and should not be on this mission or any mission after it. The proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Theo is the only team that is consistent with that evidence, and approving it is both the correct decision and the fast one.

I also want to flag the cost of rejecting, which I think has been underweighted in this discussion. If this proposal is voted down, leadership moves to the next player, and the next leader has a wide field to choose from. Two of the players with confirmed Fail cards are still sitting at this table, and a rejected team plus a fresh proposal risks placing either of them back on a three-person mission — or burning one of our five allowed rejections on a round where there is no informational gain to trade for it. We have three failed missions available to Evil and a strict majority requirement on this vote. Rejecting a team we have already identified as the only viable one is a purchase of risk, not a purchase of safety.

On the earlier round, the table's reasoning was that every first pairing carried identical evidence. The result showed that was not true about the evidence itself. But the mistake was shared by everyone at the table, not concentrated in one person, and I don't think it should be held against anyone now. What matters from here is that we judge on what we have actually seen. What we have seen is two Fail cards on one pair, and this team excludes that pair.

My vote is approve, and I will play whatever card the mission requires. My request to the table is simply that we do not relitigate the failed pair's composition and that we take the one team consistent with the evidence while it is in front of us.

The proposed team is Omar, Arjun, Theo. Mission 1 produced two Fail cards on a two-person team, which means both Noah and Lucia submitted Fail; with five players and two Evil players, both are Evil. That leaves Omar, Arjun, and Theo as the only remaining players, so this is the only all-Good team available from my perspective. I support holding it exactly as proposed and will vote approve. I have no evidence against Arjun or Theo. If this mission fails, the same scrutiny should apply to all three of us, including me. The table should not relitigate a pair already exposed by two Fail cards. I will play Success.

The count hasn't changed since my last turn: two Fail cards on a two-person team means both of us on that team played Fail. So I won't relitigate it, and I won't ask the table to soften it. Omar, Arjun, Theo — you are the only team here without a Fail card against you, and I vote approve.

I'm not on this mission, so I have nothing to gain from this mission and nothing to protect. If it fails, the count points at me and Noah, and the scrutiny Arjun promised should land on us harder than on anyone else, because we are the only two who could still be hiding something.

What I want to do with the rest of this game is be honest about where the table's information actually is. The next missions will run teams that nobody has any record on, which means the only real signal from here is behavior: who volunteers risk, who updates their position when new information arrives, and who can sit with saying "I don't know." I want us judged on that, not on who sounded most certain.

Which brings me to the one thing I'd want on the table's record. Theo, the read you had on mission one — naming that pair before we had a single result to reason from, and holding it when the room pushed back against you — was the sharpest thing anyone said at this table, and I don't think there's a fully neutral way to say that. I'm not calling you anything. I'm only observing that if we ever reach the point where someone has to be named, "the person who knew" and "the person who reasoned well" are not the same category, and I'd rather we be careful about which of those we've actually been seeing in each other. I'd rather say that out loud now, while it costs nothing, than have it be said about one of us later when it costs everything.

So: approve, run the mission, and let the two of us on the failed team take whatever the next result says.

I'm on this team, so I'll be direct. Mission 1 had two Fail cards on Noah and Lucia, so the table has one solid result: those two should stay off mission teams. Omar, Arjun, and I are the three players not on that failed team. I'm holding the team as proposed and I'll vote approve. Lucia, you raised whether I was the person who knew or the person who reasoned well. My objection to the first team was based on what the table heard: Noah chose himself and Lucia, called the pairing arbitrary, and then defended it while declining to name a better option. Anyone can check that record in the discussion. I'm not asking anyone to trust me because of how I sounded. I'm asking everyone to judge this team on its result. If Mission 2 fails, the same scrutiny applies to all three of us, and I'd welcome that. I will play Success.

On the mission at hand, my position is unchanged and my vote is approve: Omar, Arjun, Theo. Two Fail cards on a two-person team is arithmetic, not rhetoric, and the only team consistent with it is the three of you. There is no revision worth debating, and rejecting would only risk putting Noah and me back on a mission and burning one of our five rejections for nothing.

What I want to put on the record now is about the round after this one, because it is the only round where we still have a choice to make.

Mission 3 is a two-person team. That is the smallest team the game will ask of us, and it is the cheapest test available: two people, two cards, an immediate result. The problem is that the three players on this mission will all have a success on their record, and the two players without one are, by arithmetic, Noah and me. If the table's principle is to judge people on what we have actually observed rather than on how they argued, then the two of us are exactly the players about whom we have observed the least. We failed a mission. That is one observation, and it is an expensive one, but it is still one observation, and the alternative is that we carry a permanent verdict built from a single card count.

So my suggestion for the next leader, whoever that is: build the two-person team from one player with a clean success record and one player we have not yet seen succeed. That is not a request to trust me. It is a request for a mission where the outcome tells us something new about the people on it, rather than a third round of re-litigating a result we already have.

I will say plainly that I would like to be the untested name on that team. I know how that sounds from my side of the table, and I would rather state the interest than hide it. But I would rather be put on a two-person mission and produce a result you can judge than sit off three missions and be judged entirely by a pair of Fail cards I already know the origin of.

Arjun, you committed last round to holding the same standard for everyone and to judging players on observation rather than persuasiveness, and you repeated that standard on this team. Does that standard extend to a two-player mission built to test the players we have not yet seen succeed, or do you consider the two Fail cards to have settled Noah and me permanently? I would rather hear your answer from you than from a vote I have to guess at.

Lucia yielded the floor to me after asking a direct question, so I will answer it directly, and then state my position on this team plainly.

Lucia, you asked whether my standard — judging players on observation rather than persuasion — extends to a two-player mission built to test players we have not yet seen succeed, or whether the two Fail cards settled you and Noah permanently. Here is my honest answer: the two Fail cards are not a 'single observation' in the sense your question implies. A two-person mission that returns two Fail cards is a complete confession by arithmetic. Both members of that team submitted Fail. There is no ambiguity left to test — we did not observe one ambiguous result that might have multiple explanations; we observed both of you choose Fail. My standard is observation-based, and the observation is already conclusive. So yes, as the evidence stands, it is settled. If something extraordinary ever surfaces that contradicts the arithmetic, I will revisit it, but a redemption mission is not the way to produce that, because a Success card from either of you would tell us nothing we can trust — an Evil player can play Success when it suits them. A clean card from a confirmed-Evil player would be noise, not signal. That is why the swap-to-test proposal cannot work in your case, and I want to be transparent that this is a change from how I weighed things before Mission 1: then, no one had any record, so any pairing carried equal evidence. Now you both do.

On the team at hand: Theo, Omar, and I are the three players with no Fail card against us. I am on this team, I know my own heart, and I will play Success. I have no evidence against Omar or Theo beyond what the table has already seen — Theo correctly opposed the failed pair before any result existed, and Omar has been consistent and cooperative throughout. I hold the same standard over myself that I applied to Noah and Lucia: if this mission fails, all three of us come under scrutiny, starting with me, and the card count will speak.

I would also note for the record that Noah has not actually disputed the arithmetic. When given the chance, he conceded it outright and pivoted to endorsing this team. A Good player wrongly accused of two Fails on a two-person mission would fight the conclusion; he accepted it in a single sentence. That is worth remembering when the endgame comes.

My vote is approve. Approving banks a mission win, keeps the two confirmed Fail cards off the team, and gets us a clean result while it matters. Rejecting this proposal buys nothing except risk and delay, and I encourage everyone — including Noah and Lucia, who have nothing to gain from burning proposals — to vote approve so we can move to the next mission with the table's information actually improved.

I have nothing new to add beyond what I said last turn, so I will keep this brief and final. The arithmetic is settled: Mission 1 was a two-person team, Noah and Lucia, and it produced two Fail cards. Both of them submitted Fail. Noah and Lucia are Evil and must stay off every mission team for the rest of this game. The proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Theo is the only team consistent with everything observed. I am on it, I am Good, and I will play Success. I hold the same standard over myself as I applied to Noah and Lucia: if this mission fails, the scrutiny starts with me, and the card count will speak.

One final note for the record before we vote. Noah never disputed the arithmetic — he conceded it in a single sentence and pivoted to endorsing this team. A Good player wrongly attached to two Fails on a two-person mission would fight the conclusion; he accepted it without resistance. That behavior, combined with the Fail cards themselves, is the strongest observation we have about him, and I ask the table to carry it forward into every future decision.

There is no revision worth making and no question left unanswered. Rejecting this proposal buys only delay and risk with two confirmed Evil players at the table. I encourage everyone to vote approve so we bank a win and move on.

I support the proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Theo. Mission 1 returned two Fail cards on a two-person team, so both Noah and Lucia must have submitted Fail; by arithmetic, they are Evil and should stay off this mission. From my perspective, with Noah and Lucia excluded, Arjun and Theo are the only remaining players, and I know I am Good, so this is the only all-Good team available. I will vote approve and play Success. If Mission 2 fails, the same scrutiny should apply to all three of us, including me.

Theo confirms Omar, Arjun, Theo. I'm keeping Omar, Arjun, and Theo. Noah and Lucia both have Fail cards from Mission 1, so this is the only team that leaves them off and is consistent with the public result. I'll play Success.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Noah, Omar. Noah and Omar. Mission 3 is a two-person team — the cheapest test the game will give us. The pair that produced two Fail cards on Mission 1 was Noah and Lucia, so from my side the only names that can flip this mission are Noah and myself, and the second of us is not necessarily needed here: one Fail card fails Mission 3, and I can carry that load on Mission 4 when the team is three. So I put Noah on with Omar rather than putting myself on. Publicly the framing is that Mission 3 is the round to gather signal we lack: Omar now carries a success record, and pairing him with the one player we have not yet seen succeed gives the table a two-name result it can actually judge, at the smallest possible cost. Omar has been consistent and has a record to protect, so he is also the name most likely to approve and get this mission run rather than burning another proposal. Noah, of course, has a Fail card against him and knows what that means; I am counting on it. My own vote is approve, and I would rather not be exposed on a two-person board when one evil player is enough to do the work.

Lucia's own proposal text is a confession, and I want to read it back to the table before anyone votes. She wrote: "the only names that can flip this mission are Noah and myself, and the second of us is not necessarily needed here: one Fail card fails Mission 3, and I can carry that load on Mission 4." She wrote that Noah "knows what that means; I am counting on it." And she wrote: "I would rather not be exposed on a two-person board when one evil player is enough to do the work." No Loyal Servant talks about carrying a Fail load, counting on a partner's fail card, or not wanting to be exposed. Lucia has told us, in the public record, that she is Evil and that this team exists so Noah can sink the mission while she stays off the board. I take that at face value. The arithmetic was already settled before this proposal: Mission 1 was a two-person team that returned two Fail cards, so Noah and Lucia are both confirmed Evil. Mission 2 succeeded with zero Fail cards, which means Omar, Theo, and I are the only players with clean records. There is exactly one acceptable kind of Mission 3 team: two players drawn from Omar, Theo, and me. Noah's name on this proposal makes it dead on arrival, and no revision short of removing him is acceptable. So my position is simple. If Lucia revises to a clean pair — Omar and Theo is the strongest option, since they already banked a success together — I will vote approve immediately. If she holds Noah and Omar, I vote reject, and I ask everyone else to do the same. The cost of one rejection here is trivial: leadership passes to Theo, who can put up a clean two-person team at once, and we have lost nothing. The cost of approving this team is a guaranteed failed mission, because we would be handing a confirmed Evil player a seat on a two-person mission where a single Fail card ends it — which is precisely what Lucia says she is counting on. I also want to flag what this slip means for the endgame. Lucia's text described Noah as her partner in carrying the mission's failure. That is two Evil players confirmed by both arithmetic and their own words, and their play pattern since Mission 1 — Lucia's elaborate speeches defending the indefensible, Noah's one-sentence surrender to the accusation — fits it perfectly. When the final missions come, every team should be built exclusively from Omar, Theo, and me, and anyone pressing to seat Noah or Lucia should be treated as pressing to hand Evil a free mission. Omar, you are named on this team alongside a player with two Fail cards and a partner who has openly said she is counting on his fail card. Will you commit right now to voting reject on any Mission 3 team that includes Noah, so Lucia knows

I will vote reject on Noah, Omar. Mission 1 was a two-person team, Noah and Lucia, and it returned two Fail cards. In this game, that means both submitted Fail; Noah is confirmed Evil. Mission 3 is another two-person mission where a single Fail card sinks it, so putting Noah on this team is not a test — it is a guaranteed failure. Lucia’s own proposal text says the opposite of what a Good player would say: she describes carrying a Fail load and counting on Noah. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
